candidates.title: The Blue Economy: The World’s Quietest Economic Engine And Its Smartest Cities
candidates.snippet: The $2.6 trillion blue economy is creating startup opportunities in maritime automation, clean energy and logistics, with blue tech funding nearing $10 billion through Q3 2026, driven largely by major defense deals. Alberto Onetti, chairman of Mind the Bridge, writes that ports are emerging as hubs for testing and scaling these technologies, but realizing their potential requires coordination among port authorities, startups, investors and policymakers.

The Blue Economy: The World’s Quietest Economic Engine And Its Smartest Cities

By Alberto Onetti
The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy.
For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources.
Alberto Onetti, Mind The Bridge
The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central.
Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea.
Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge ’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge.
Blue tech: A sector defying global slowdown
Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end.
The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end.
The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026).
Not all blue tech is the same
Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups.
We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density).
The result is a matrix highlighting:
Transformational technologies that have a high impact and are relatively well-established. Among those, AI and machine learning, and robotics and industrial automation occupies a particular sweet spot of high impact, substantial investment and high scaleup density (more than 200 scaleups and $20 billion invested in total).
High-potential disruptive technologies, with only relatively lower levels of investment and scaleup density (roughly 50 scaleups and $3 billion to $5 billion invested per cluster). Among them, the most promising ones are maritime clean propulsion and sustainable fuels, and supply chain and freight tech.
The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies.
Ports: the ‘smartest smart cities’
The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy?
Short answer: ports.
Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy.
And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook.
To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation.
While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy.
The result is a picture that shows the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy.
To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units.
Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges.
Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona , a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge .
Notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them.

candidates.title: What’s Next For Recruiting, Job Hunting And HR? More AI, Of Course
candidates.snippet: So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

What’s Next For Recruiting, Job Hunting And HR? More AI, Of Course

Joanna Glasner

AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.
So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.
To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.
Top fundraisers
Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.
As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.
By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor , a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.
San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.
The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob , a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce 1 -led financing.
Startups focused on jobseekers
Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.
In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox , an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.
Agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview , a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI , which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.
Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform , announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.
Surprisingly depressing
So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?
Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.
Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.
Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

Payhawk, the London-headquartered spend management company founded in Bulgaria, announced a $280 million Series C on Wednesday, Nov. 18, led by the growth equity team at Goldman Sachs Alternatives at a $2 billion valuation, to build AI finance agents that do finance work on top of payments infrastructure and enterprise controls, FinTech Global reported .
For finance leaders weighing agentic tools, the third layer to examine is enterprise controls over agent actions that set what an agent may do and when a person must step in. The announcement does not describe how that approval design works, and the round remains subject to standard regulatory approvals .
Goldman Sachs Alternatives Leads $280M Round at $2B, Subject to Regulatory Approvals
Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives led the all-equity round, which takes Payhawk's total funding past $500 million, according to TechCrunch ; FinTech Global puts the total above $515 million . Existing investors include QED, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures. FinTech Global lists four new backers, Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus, plus European founders Tomas Okmanas and Didac Lee. James Hayward, a managing director at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, will join Payhawk's board .
The valuation doubles the $1 billion Payhawk reached in March 2022, when a $100 million Lightspeed-led extension lifted its Series B to $215 million and made it Bulgaria's first unicorn. The earlier $112 million Series B tranche , led by Greenoaks in November 2021 at a $570 million valuation, came first. A $20 million Series A led by QED in April 2021 preceded it, following a €3 million (approximately $3.3 million) seed round in March 2020.
Bloomberg reported on Jan. 7, as summarized by Let's Data Science , that Payhawk was in talks to raise more than $100 million at about a $2 billion valuation. The valuation held while the round grew to $280 million, roughly 2.8 times the reported floor. TechCrunch, citing Sifted, said the round was one of Europe's largest Series C rounds this year.
Finance OS Stacks AI Agents on Payments Infrastructure and Enterprise Controls
Payhawk describes its Finance Operating System as three connected layers : AI agents that carry out financial work, payments infrastructure that lets those agents handle money, and enterprise controls that limit what an agent may do and trigger human intervention when needed. CEO Hristo Borisov's distinction, as Securities.io reports it , is that integrations connect systems, while an operating system changes how the entire finance function works.
The agents are not new; the stack around them is the pitch. Payhawk announced its AI Office of the CFO suite of four agents on April 2, 2025, with the Financial Controller Agent first in early access, and said the agents work with "the same careful permissions as employees" under existing approval workflows, spend controls and audit trails. Fintech Times reported on Sept. 25, 2025, that Payhawk's Fall '25 Product Edition launched four agents covering financial control, procurement, travel and payments, and that the Procurement Agent can route approvals, raise card limits or create purchase orders, with agent actions logged for auditability.
Underneath sits a payments footprint built before the AI pivot. Payhawk became a Visa principal member in 2023, which Fintech Times said lets it issue Visa cards directly rather than depend on outside partners, and Borisov said then that, with its e-money license, Payhawk could "control more of the payment processing stack." Payhawk's help page lists e-money licenses from the Bank of Lithuania dated July 11, 2023, and the UK Financial Conduct Authority dated Jan. 13, 2024. None of the announcement coverage says whether agent spending limits are enforced inside Payhawk's card and payments systems or only in its approval workflow, a question finance buyers can put to the company directly.

Agent Fetch, a capability of Payhawk's Financial Controller Agent, shows the mechanism at small scale. An employee authorizes the agent once through an encrypted session, and Payhawk says it never stores portal passwords. The agent then signs into connected supplier portals, retrieves invoices, extracts the data, posts it to Payhawk and matches it to the payment . Payhawk says the agent is verified through Cloudflare's Verified Bots program , which lets websites identify it as authorized automated traffic.
Payhawk's July 21 release said it is rolling out Agent Fetch to its entire customer base after a beta in which more than 550 businesses activated it, and reported that after login the agent retrieved invoices autonomously in 68.6% of attempts, up to 12 times faster than people. The company also said its Financial Controller Agent has cut the time to submit supplier-invoice expenses by up to 46% since the start of 2026, taking the time for an invoice to reach the ERP system from as much as 23.8 days to 12.6 days against a two-day target, The Paypers reported . SUZHOU, China , Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MegaRobo Technologies (MegaRobo), a technology company building Intelligence Infrastructure for the Physical World, today announced that it has raised nearly US$200 million in a new financing round joined by Oman Investment Authority (OIA), the sovereign wealth fund of the Sultanate of Oman. And existing investors Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia and Sinovation Ventures continued to back the company, with new participation from CMB International.
The new financing will support MegaRobo's continued investment in core technology, the global expansion of its AI for Science business, and the development of infrastructure that enables AI to operate in increasingly complex physical environments.
AI's Next Frontier Is the Physical World
The first generation of AI learned primarily from digital information - text, images, video and code. The next generation will increasingly learn by interacting with the physical world: acting on real systems, observing outcomes, and using those outcomes to decide what to do next.
In science, that means moving beyond reading papers, predicting structures or generating molecules. AI must also be able to design experiments, execute them in real laboratories, observe the results and learn from what happens.
MegaRobo is building the infrastructure for that transition. Its proprietary One Intelligence Stack connects intelligence with execution - bringing together models and agents, data, workflows, software, scientific instruments, robotics, automation and real-world feedback in a single reusable technology foundation.
One Intelligence Stack. Across Complex Physical Systems.
THINK → DESIGN → EXECUTE → OBSERVE → LEARN
Science Is Where It Begins
Science is the first proving ground for this architecture because it requires AI to do more than analyze information. Scientific discovery depends on an ongoing loop between reasoning, design, physical experimentation, observation and learning - often under conditions where the answer is not known in advance.
MegaRobo is applying this architecture to scientific discovery and pharmaceutical R&D through an integrated AI for Science infrastructure that combines AI, scientific computing, experimental execution, data and R&D decision-making.
The company has delivered products and technologies to more than 500 customers, including leading global pharmaceutical companies, drug discovery organizations, biotechnology companies and research institutions. Its systems support key stages of discovery and development, including early research, target and mechanism discovery, drug screening and candidate optimization.
Through Megalaxy Lab, MegaRobo is also making real-world experimentation increasingly programmable. Researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them to automated laboratory systems, track execution, and receive structured, machine-readable results that can feed directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning. Megalaxy Lab has served more than 200 customers.
MegaRobo is now extending this capability to the global AI for Science community. Together with industry partners including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience, the company has launched Poreva Open, a global AI protein design challenge open to all models and technical approaches. Megalaxy Lab will provide wet-lab validation for more than 10,000 protein design sequences, creating an opportunity for innovators worldwide to test their models against real experimental results. By opening up large-scale experimental validation to the global research community, Poreva Open aims to help establish a common benchmark for AI-driven protein design.
This marks a shift in how scientific infrastructure is accessed: from laboratory work organized mainly as individual projects toward experimental capacity that can increasingly be standardized, automated and called on demand by scientists, software and AI agents.
A Reusable Foundation for Complex Physical Systems
Science is where MegaRobo is starting, but the underlying architecture is designed for other complex physical systems as well. Wherever AI must interact with instruments, machines, materials, processes and real-world feedback, the same core challenge appears: intelligence must connect to execution, and execution must generate observations that intelligence can learn from.
MegaRobo is developing One Intelligence Stack as a common technology foundation for this interaction - not as a collection of isolated AI applications or automation products, but as infrastructure that enables AI to act, observe and learn across complex physical environments.
Daniel Huang, Founder and CEO of MegaRobo, said: "The first generation of AI learned from humanity's accumulated knowledge. The next generation will increasingly learn by acting in the physical world - through experiments, production and continuous feedback. That shift changes AI from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create new knowledge, materials, processes and products. MegaRobo is building the infrastructure for that transition."

WATERTOWN, Mass.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Marrow Therapeutics , a platform company developing novel bone marrow-targeted therapies to treat severe blood disorders, today announced its launch with a combined $173 million in Series A and B funding. The $53 million Series A financing was co-led by Scion Life Sciences and venBio. The $120 million Series B round was led by OrbiMed, with participation from all Series A investors and new funds, including RTW Investments, Surveyor Capital (a Citadel company), Opaleye, NEXTBio Capital, Affinity Advisors, KKR, Spruce Street Capital and Columbia Threadneedle Investments. Art Levin, founding Chief Scientific Officer of Avidity Biosciences, and Stuart Orkin, David G. Nathan Distinguished Professor of Pediatrics at Harvard Medical School and HHMI Investigator at Boston Children’s Hospital, have joined the Board and SAB, respectively.
Marrow is pioneering a novel approach for genetic disease therapy by developing engineered antibodies through its first-in-class and potentially best-in-class bone marrow targeting platform. Marrow’s engineered antibodies precisely target the transferrin receptor (TfR1) in bone marrow and deliver therapeutic payloads to bone marrow to treat severe blood disorders. The company’s in vivo approach aims to achieve efficacy while overcoming critical limitations of earlier genetic medicine approaches, such as safety concerns, manufacturing complexity and patient accessibility.
Marrow is advancing multiple programs utilizing their proprietary Transferrin Antibody Bioconjugate (TAB) platform, targeting a range of hematological and bone marrow diseases. The company’s lead candidate, MAR-101, currently in IND-enabling studies, is designed to treat both sickle cell disease (SCD) and beta thalassemia by decreasing BCL11a and reactivating fetal hemoglobin production.
“We’re at a pivotal moment in genetic medicine and its application in severe blood disorders – the field has validated key targets and shown that genetic approaches can work, but we need to solve the safety and accessibility challenges to truly transform patient outcomes,” said Romesh Subramanian, Marrow Therapeutics’ President and Chief Executive Officer. “By precisely targeting the bone marrow, we’re able to deliver the potential of genetic medicines and provide sustained benefit, while simultaneously avoiding the risks that have constrained earlier approaches. Our preclinical data gives us tremendous confidence in this strategy, and we’re excited to move toward the clinic with a platform designed to address a broad range of severe hematological diseases.”
The company’s platform is built on deep scientific and technical expertise and extensive experience with the transferrin receptor, understanding precisely how to engage it for therapeutic benefit while avoiding off-target effects, particularly the anemia risk that limits other TfR1-targeted approaches. In addition to President and CEO Romesh Subramanian, the company has appointed Tim Weeden as Chief Scientific Officer, bringing extensive experience in transferrin receptor biology, antibody and nucleic acid development; John Najim as Chief Operating Officer and Chief Technology Officer, bringing expertise in chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC) and operations; and Gavriel Mullokandov as Founder and VP, Corporate Development to support the development and advancement of the company’s programs and platform.
“Marrow represents a differentiated technology platform, experienced leadership, and the potential to provide effective and safe treatment options for severe blood disorders,” said Mona Ashiya, General Partner, OrbiMed. “I am excited to work with this experienced team that has brought first-generation TfR1 platforms into the clinic. What is particularly compelling is their ‘pipeline in a product’ strategy. MAR-101 validates the platform across sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia with a single therapeutic approach, while their growing pipeline across additional blood and bone disorders demonstrates the true versatility and long-term value of this platform.”
“From its inception, Marrow has had the potential to become a transformative and valuable company. This has been made possible by an experienced and knowledgeable leadership team that has consistently displayed the scientific rigor and operational excellence we look for at Scion. Marrow has optimized its proprietary bone marrow-targeting platform using lessons learned from validated first-generation TfR1 platforms targeting other tissues and organs. By leveraging well-understood biology, the company is in a great position to create paradigm-shifting therapies for patients dealing with severe blood disorders of high unmet need,” said Aaron Kantoff, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Scion Life Sciences. “We are truly excited to see Marrow advance its programs into the clinic in the coming year.”

Marrow Therapeutics is a genetic medicines company developing a proprietary, bone marrow-targeted platform to treat severe blood disorders. The company’s Transferrin Antibody Bioconjugate (TAB) platform delivers therapeutic payloads directly to bone marrow cells to enable safe and effective treatment of hematological diseases, including sickle cell disease, beta thalassemia and other blood disorders. SAN FRANCISCO , Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Linq , the infrastructure platform for AI agents, today announced $90 million in new funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, with continued participation from TQ Ventures, Mucker Capital, and Abstract, and new participation from Anthos and Left Lane Capital. Ben Horowitz will join its board of directors.
Continue Reading
Linq’s Co-Founders: Patrick Sullivan (CTO), Elliott Potter (CEO), and Jared Mattsson (President)
The internet gave every business a website. The iPhone gave every business an app. Now AI is giving every business, and every person, an agent. Cloudflare reports that more than half of internet traffic is no longer human, with AI agent requests on its network up more than 1,700% in a year. These are not simple, customer-service chatbots: these agents book, buy, and make plans by communicating with people and using software on their behalf.
Messaging was Linq's first product and remains a core part of its growing AI infrastructure platform. As the provider for DoorDash, Town, Tomo, and hundreds of others, Linq has already processed more than 1 billion messages. DoorDash uses Linq to help customers find food, build a cart, and check out in a single thread. And now, as an Apple Messaging Service Provider, Linq can help more enterprises launch and scale customer-facing agents on the same channel.
"The best AI experiences fit naturally into people's lives," said Aryan Shah, Head of AI research at DoorDash. "Linq gives us the messaging infrastructure to bring ordering into a familiar conversation, so customers can go from deciding what they want to placing an order in one thread."
"Agents will communicate and get work done just like people do. Linq gives agents the infrastructure to do both at scale," said Ben Horowitz, cofounder and general partner at Andreessen Horowitz.
Messaging is the beginning of a larger shift: people will describe what they need, and agents will get it done. Linq's computer use offering gives agents access to physical computing infrastructure to interact with software and complete tasks. HD Calling for Agents adds voice calling to the platform. Pulley , a technology company providing AI-powered permitting and development services, has raised $64 million in funding to expand its platform and introduce new products designed to accelerate commercial real estate development.
The financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital , with participation from Catalyst Investors , and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures. The announcement follows fivefold year-over-year growth in Pulley’s annual recurring revenue.
The company plans to use the capital to expand its permitting operations and develop tools that help businesses evaluate potential development sites, navigate regulatory requirements and identify construction design issues before submitting projects for approval.
Pulley provides permitting services to major retailers, restaurants, financial institutions, manufacturers and data center operators. Its customers include Amazon, Starbucks, JLL, Meta and Equinix.
The company combines artificial intelligence, regulatory data and a nationwide team of more than 75 licensed professionals to help customers manage construction approvals across all 50 states.
According to Pulley, its platform has supported more than $21 billion in commercial construction projects and helped customers save a combined 11,750 weeks of project development time.
“The speed at which we build is one of the most important challenges facing America over the next decade,” said Charlie Jacobson , co-founder and CEO of Pulley. “To remain a global leader in AI, bring manufacturing back home, reach energy independence and sustain job growth, we need to build orders of magnitude faster. The single biggest lever to building faster is to get started faster.”
Pulley’s existing services include regulatory due diligence, permitting strategy development, construction plan reviews and coordination with local government agencies.
The company also participates in private plan review programs covering more than 2,000 cities and counties, allowing its certified professionals to approve building plans in jurisdictions that authorize private review.
Pulley said its customers typically receive one round of jurisdictional review comments per project, while more than 40% of projects receive approval without any comments. The company also reported a 65% reduction in review comments in 2026 compared with 2025.
“Pulley’s understanding of jurisdictional requirements and code interpretations helps us anticipate issues before design is complete,” said Karen Rojas , design, development and delivery manager at Meta. “As we move toward a single partner managing permitting from site development through construction, Pulley is helping shape our approach.”
The new funding will support Pulley’s expansion beyond permitting into earlier stages of real estate development.
Planned capabilities include site selection tools that combine zoning and permitting regulations with information about utility availability, local community sentiment and other development constraints.
Pulley is also introducing AI-powered construction drawing reviews intended to identify building code compliance issues during the design process, reducing the need for revisions after plans are submitted to regulatory authorities.
The company said its broader objective is to create an integrated platform that helps developers make site selection, design and permitting decisions within a single system.
“Pulley has demonstrated a rare ability to transform essential but historically fragmented work into a scalable technology solution,” said Sach Chitnis , co-founder and partner at Jump Capital. “The company has built deep expertise, strong customer relationships and a differentiated intelligence layer that becomes more valuable with every project.”
Pulley said its permitting service can help enterprises secure construction approvals up to 70% faster by combining AI agents with regulatory intelligence and specialized permitting professionals.
The company did not disclose its valuation or provide a timeline for the full commercial rollout of its new development planning products.

Ashish and I still remember the incident-response war rooms after the SolarWinds supply chain attack in Dec 2020. Ashish was at Uber and I was at Microsoft. We were trying to answer two questions: were we affected and how would we prevent an attack like this from happening again? The cybersecurity solutions we had relied on offered frustratingly little help with the questions in front of us. Our teams scrambled to piece together the answers and build homegrown workarounds under high pressure.
A few months later, attackers inserted malicious code into Codecov’s Bash Uploader, bringing the same scramble back. The malicious code stole secrets from customers’ CI/CD environments for roughly two months before it was discovered.
The security tools we relied on focused on vulnerabilities attackers might exploit in production. These attacks exposed a different risk. Malicious code could cause damage on a developer’s machine or in a CI/CD pipeline. It did not need to reach production.
Those experiences drove us to start StepSecurity in 2021. We wanted security teams to have visibility and protection in the environments where software gets built.
We raised our seed round of $3 million in May 2024. Since then, our ARR grew 5× in 2024 and again in 2025. In 2026, we have already crossed that 5× growth milestone and are on pace for our biggest growth year yet.
More than 20,000 open-source projects now use our Harden-Runner community tier. Enterprise customers including Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercor, Mercari, Chainguard, and XBOW trust StepSecurity to protect their software supply chains.
Today, we’re announcing an oversubscribed $20 million Series A led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital, and SaaS Ventures.
The problem that led us to start StepSecurity has grown more urgent and now extends to every knowledge worker. Any knowledge worker can ask an AI agent to perform a task, such as creating a spreadsheet. To complete it, the agent may download open-source packages and execute code.
Software is now built everywhere: by agents on laptops, in the cloud, and inside pipelines. That creates a larger attack surface, even as AI makes attacks easier to launch.
Recent attacks show how developer tools and workstations can expose sensitive systems. Examples include the tampered Claude Code extension in Cursor’s marketplace and Binance’s reported breach.
This funding will strengthen the protection our products provide for developer machines, package downloads, and CI/CD. It will also help us build protection for agent sandboxes.

Ashish and I met at Microsoft in 2009. I went on to lead the Green Team within Azure Security, focused on making security easy for developers. Ashish built Uber’s cloud security function and later led infrastructure security at Plaid, securing cloud environments and the systems developers used to build and deliver software. We had lived with the challenge of protecting those environments while helping developers get their work done.
We saw attackers shifting left into the systems used to build and deliver software by compromising trusted open-source components that many enterprises used. From their perspective, it made sense: compromise one component, and they could reach many organizations at once.
The security tools we had relied on were built primarily to defend against attacks in production. Even application security tools used during development largely reflected that threat model. The threat model behind traditional software composition analysis (SCA) focused only on vulnerabilities.
In a typical scenario, an open-source developer makes an honest mistake that introduces a vulnerability into their project. A security researcher or threat actor then discovers that vulnerability. To compromise an enterprise using this vulnerability, the vulnerable component would need to move from a developer’s machine into a code repository, through the CI/CD pipeline, and all the way into production. An attacker would then need to exploit the flaw in the running application over a network connection.
SolarWinds and Codecov exposed a different problem: attackers had deliberately planted malicious code in trusted software. This meant the compromised component did not need to reach production. It only needed to execute somewhere in the software development and delivery pipeline, such as a developer’s machine or a CI/CD job, to exfiltrate secrets. Attackers then used those stolen credentials to access production systems and data. None of the security tools we relied on were monitoring these points in the pipeline for this kind of attack.

AI governance and assurance startup Disseqt AI has raised $8 million in pre-Series A funding round led by Gresham House Ventures, with participation from existing investor Sure Valley Ventures (SVV), Delta Partners and Enterprise Ireland.
The round also saw participation from angel investors, including senior executives from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta, along with former Indian cricket captain Rahul Dravid, who invested in his individual capacity.

Its platform enables businesses to assess AI agents for vulnerabilities before deployment, enforce company policies once they go live, and continuously monitor their behaviour. It can also block outputs that violate organisational policies while maintaining audit trails for compliance and oversight.

Disseqt said it has already deployed its assurance capabilities across multiple enterprise use cases. It added that no unsafe outputs were detected when the original failing tests were repeated after fixes.
The company also provides assurance services for a credit card services programme at a large European bank.
The investment marks another bet on the emerging AI governance and assurance segment, as enterprises look to deploy autonomous AI systems across customer interactions, financial services and internal business operations.

Prepared by the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM), the report highlights Bengaluru's position in India's startup ecosystem, covering funding, deep tech, AI, unicorns, women entrepreneurs, IPOs and emerging technology hubs across Karnataka.
Presenting the report, Siddarth Pai, founding partner of 3one4 Capital, said Karnataka's digital economy was valued at $159 billion and was projected to reach nearly $400 billion by 2031-32. The state accounted for 47% of India's venture capital funding between 2016 and 2026, amounting to $85 billion, the report said.
Of the 1,556 deep-tech startups founded in Bengaluru since 2010, 1,319 are active and funded, having raised a total of $3.77 billion. The city also has 799 native AI startups, of which 764 are active and funded.
Bengaluru-based startups have raised around $85 billion since 2010, accounting for 47% of the total venture funding raised by Indian startups. Of this, $76.5 billion was raised in the past decade. The city has 3,810 active, funded startups founded since 2010, nearly twice Mumbai's 1,982.
The report puts the combined valuation of Bengaluru's 57 unicorns at $211 billion. They account for 44% of India's 131 unicorns and 55.3% of their combined valuation. Bengaluru has produced 46 of India's 100 unicorns since 2020, with startups taking an average of six years to attain unicorn status.
The city also has 212 soonicorns, accounting for 36% of India's total of 589, ahead of Delhi NCR (134) and Mumbai (121). Bengaluru startups take around five years to reach soonicorn status.
Nearly 30% of India's active, funded women-led deep-tech and native AI startups were founded in Bengaluru. These companies have collectively raised $323.65 million, the report said.
Bengaluru also accounts for a significant share of startup listings. Sixteen companies linked to the city have been listed since November 2024, with a combined valuation of around $42 billion at the time of listing. Bengaluru accounts for 33 of the 226 IPOs by funded companies in India during this period, while Karnataka-headquartered companies account for 37, or around 16%.
Startups in Bengaluru take an average of 8.2 years from founding to exit, compared with the global average of 11.1 years. Karnataka has around 300 venture capital firms, while Bengaluru is home to 75 Category I Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), accounting for 21% of India's total and ranking second after Mumbai.
The median seed funding round in Bengaluru is $810,000, while the median Series A round is $5.9 million. Domestic investors now contribute 52% of the capital raised by Category I and II AIFs. Ten family offices in Bengaluru are active in deep tech, with 57 equity-round participations in deep tech and 45 in native AI.
The report also highlighted efforts to expand Karnataka's startup ecosystem beyond Bengaluru. Kharge said the state's next task was to help companies working in AI, quantum computing and semiconductors grow in other cities, including Kalaburagi, Hubballi and Mangaluru. He added that deep-tech development required patient investment and the state would continue to support the sector.

Founded by entrepreneurs born in 1999, Vietnamese startup Vucar has secured another multimillion-dollar investment to expand its AI-powered used car valuation and online auction platform.
Vietnamese technology startup Vucar has completed a Pre-Series A funding round led by OSK-SBI Venture Partners, with existing investors Monk's Hill Ventures of Singapore and Antler also participating.
Founded in Ho Chi Minh City in 2023 by a group of entrepreneurs born in 1999, Vucar operates a platform combining artificial intelligence (AI), on-site vehicle inspections and online auctions to simplify used car transactions.
The company did not disclose the exact funding amount, but a representative said the investment could reach several million US dollars.
Vucar previously raised a million-dollar seed funding round in September 2024. The latest investment signals continued international investor interest in its business model and expansion potential in Vietnam's used car market.
AI-powered valuations based on over 4 million data points
Vucar's founders, all born in 1999, have secured another multimillion-dollar funding round for their used car trading platform. Photo: Vucar
Determining a fair selling price remains one of the biggest challenges in Vietnam's used car market.
Even vehicles of the same model, production year and variant can command significantly different prices depending on mileage, engine condition, bodywork, maintenance history and market demand.
Overpricing can leave a vehicle unsold for an extended period, while undervaluing it can result in financial losses for the owner. Buyers also face difficulties assessing whether asking prices accurately reflect a vehicle's condition.
Vucar has developed an AI-powered valuation tool using more than 4 million data points to generate indicative prices based on each vehicle's characteristics and condition.
Rather than relying solely on advertised prices across online marketplaces, the system aims to provide faster market insights and help owners estimate their vehicles' value before deciding to sell.
The startup has also introduced an AI assistant that answers questions from buyers and sellers about individual vehicles, reducing response times and easing the workload of customer service staff.
However, Vucar does not rely entirely on algorithms.
Physical inspections, document verification, contract assistance and vehicle handovers remain the responsibility of its employees.
"AI helps us value cars faster and respond to customers almost instantly. But no algorithm can replace someone who visits the vehicle in person and supports the customer until payment is received. Car sellers need both," said Jake Vu, CEO and co-founder of Vucar.
The company's sales process is designed to minimize the tasks owners must handle themselves.
Sellers submit their vehicle information through Vucar's website, after which a company specialist conducts a free on-site inspection.
The inspection results are recorded before the vehicle is listed on an online auction platform, where multiple prospective buyers can submit competing bids.
Owners can accept the highest offer or reject the transaction if the price does not meet their expectations.
Once an agreement is reached, Vucar assists with documentation, payment and vehicle handover.
The company says it charges a 1% fee only when a transaction is successfully completed.
Unlike traditional used car dealerships, Vucar does not purchase vehicles for resale. Instead, it acts as an intermediary connecting sellers with a network of buyers.
According to company figures, the platform receives more than 8,500 customer inquiries and organizes over 2,000 auctions each month.
Some transactions can be completed in approximately 27 hours, a relatively short period for a market where sales often involve extensive inspections, negotiations and administrative procedures.

Toyota is looking beyond the automotive industry as it places bigger bets on robotics, physical AI, energy, aerospace, and other emerging technologies. Through its venture arm, Woven Capital , the automaker is investing in startups that could help shape what the company looks like decades from now. But as startup valuations climb and competition for promising companies intensifies, figuring out where the next big opportunities lie is becoming increasingly important.
On this episode of TechCrunch’s ⁠Equity⁠ podcast, transportation editor Kirsten Korosec is joined by ⁠Ro Gupta⁠ , head of ⁠Woven Capital⁠ and former founder of autonomous vehicle startup Carmera, to discuss Toyota’s investment strategy, the changing venture capital landscape, and what’s next for emerging technology. Listen to the full episode to hear about:
Why Ro thinks today’s sky-high startup valuations may be more justified than they first appear, and whether there are enough worthwhile companies to warrant the investment.
How the autonomous vehicle boom of 2017 and 2018 compares to today’s AI frenzy, and why future technology hype cycles could move faster.
Why Toyota is investing beyond its traditional automotive business, from robotics and physical AI to energy, aerospace, and manufacturing.
What Woven Capital looks for in startups, why manufacturing and supply chain technology are suddenly attracting attention, and how Toyota’s industrial expertise can give portfolio companies an advantage.
Why corporate venture capital has become more attractive to founders, and how strategic investors can offer more than just money through customers, manufacturing capabilities, and global distribution.
Where the next opportunities in autonomous vehicles are emerging, and why the biggest investments may now be in the infrastructure and operations that make autonomous fleets work at scale.
